Fix an integer $d\ge1$, independent real random variables
$Y_1,\ldots,Y_d$ with marginal Borel probability laws $\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_d$,
and a degree cutoff vector $p=(p_1,\ldots,p_d)\in\mathbb N_0^d$. Their joint
law is $\rho=\rho_1\otimes\cdots\otimes\rho_d$, as in
[[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]]. Write
$\Gamma=\prod_{j=1}^d\operatorname{supp}(\rho_j)$, with the product Borel
sigma-algebra. The cutoff vector $p$ is **admissible** when, for every
$j=1,\ldots,d$,
$$\int |y|^{2p_j}\,d\rho_j(y)<\infty$$
and the monomial Gram matrix
$$G_j=(\int y^{r+s}\,d\rho_j(y))_{0\le r,s\le p_j}$$
is positive definite, meaning $c^T G_jc>0$ for each nonzero
$c\in\mathbb R^{p_j+1}$. Throughout the pair, assume the selected cutoff
vector is admissible. The admissible degree box is
$\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^d:0\le\alpha_j\le p_j\text{ for every }j\}$.
Admissibility gives a finite inner product on each stated polynomial space.
It is only a finite-degree condition; it does not assert that polynomials are
dense in any $L^2(\rho_j)$.

Let $(v_0,\ldots,v_{r-1})$ be a finite linearly independent list in a real or complex inner product space. There is an orthonormal list $(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$ such that, for every $k\le r$,

$$\operatorname{span}(e_0,\ldots,e_{k-1})=\operatorname{span}(v_0,\ldots,v_{k-1}).$$

It is obtained recursively from

$$u_k=v_k-\sum_{j<k}\langle v_k,e_j\rangle e_j,\qquad e_k=\frac{u_k}{\lVert u_k\rVert}.$$

For $r=0$, both lists are empty.

For a vector $v$ in a real or complex inner product space, define its **inner-product norm** by

$$\lVert v\rVert:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}.$$

Positive definiteness in [[def-inner-product-space]] makes the radicand a nonnegative real, and [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] supplies its unique nonnegative square root. The notation therefore defines one real number $\lVert v\rVert\ge0$. Its norm axioms are established in [[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]].

derivations.claim: Let $\mathcal P_{p_j}$ be the real vector space spanned by the formal monomials $1,y,\ldots,y^{p_j}$. For $q,r\in\mathcal P_{p_j}$ define $\langle q,r\rangle_{\rho_j}:=\int q(y)r(y)\,d\rho_j(y)$. Every product $qr$ has degree at most $2p_j$ and is integrable by [F2], so the pairing is finite; linearity of the integral makes it bilinear and symmetric. If $q(y)=\sum_{r=0}^{p_j}c_ry^r$, then $\langle q,q\rangle_{\rho_j}=c^TG_jc$, which is positive for each nonzero formal polynomial by [F1]. Thus this is an inner product on $\mathcal P_{p_j}$.

Every $q\in\mathcal P_{p_j}$ has finite squared integral by [F2], so it defines an $L^2(\rho_j)$ class. If that class is zero, then $q=0$ almost everywhere and $\int q^2\,d\rho_j=0$; by [F1] its coefficient vector must be zero. Thus the class map is injective and the monomial classes are linearly independent. The formal monomials are also independent by uniqueness of their coefficient lists, so [F3] applies to this list in $\mathcal P_{p_j}$. Its residual at stage $k$ is $y^k$ minus a polynomial of degree at most $k-1$, so it has degree $k$ and leading coefficient $1$.

Each residual is nonzero in $\mathcal P_{p_j}$ by its degree and leading coefficient, so [F4] makes its norm strictly positive. The normalized residual is orthogonal to the preceding polynomials and has positive leading coefficient. At $k=0$, the residual is $1$ and its norm is $\sqrt{\int1\,d\rho_j}=1$ because $\rho_j$ is a probability law; hence $\phi_{j,0}=1$. This proves the stated finite orthonormal family.

Let $(\Gamma,\mathcal B(\Gamma),\rho)$ be the finite product-law probability
space of [[def-finite-product-chaos-input]], and let $V$ be a separable real
Hilbert space. Define $L^2_\rho(V)$ to be the space of strongly measurable
maps $U:\Gamma\to V$ for which
$\int_\Gamma\|U(y)\|_V^2\,d\rho(y)<\infty$, modulo equality
$\rho$-almost everywhere. Its inner product is
$$ (U,W)_{L^2_\rho(V)}=\int_\Gamma (U(y),W(y))_V\,d\rho(y). $$

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $f,g\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_p\le\|f\|_p+\|g\|_p.$$
2. If $f,g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_\infty\le\|f\|_\infty+\|g\|_\infty.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, let $B$ be a separable
Banach space, and let $f:\Omega\to B$ be Borel-measurable. Then $f$ is strongly
measurable: outside a $P$-null set it is the pointwise limit of finite-valued
measurable simple functions.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: For $U,W\in L^2_\rho(V)$, pointwise Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|(U(y),W(y))_V|\le\|U(y)\|_V\|W(y)\|_V$. Integrating and applying [F3] shows that the product is integrable and the pairing is finite. Changing either representative on a null set does not change the integral. The pairing is bilinear and symmetric. If its value on $(U,U)$ is zero, then for each integer $n\ge1$ the set $E_n=\{y:\|U(y)\|_V\ge1/n\}$ has measure zero, since $0=\int\|U\|^2\ge\rho(E_n)/n^2$; their countable union contains every point where $U\ne0$. Thus the class of $U$ is zero, proving positive definiteness.

Let $(U_n)$ be Cauchy in the displayed norm. By [A1] select a subsequence $(U_{n_k})$ with $\|U_{n_{k+1}}-U_{n_k}\|_{L^2_\rho(V)}\le2^{-k}$. By [A2], choose strongly measurable representatives for these countably many classes and simple-approximation witnesses for each representative; replace each representative by zero on its measurable null exceptional set, obtaining Borel versions of the same classes. Put $d_k(y)=\|U_{n_{k+1}}(y)-U_{n_k}(y)\|_V$ and $s_m=\sum_{k=1}^m d_k$. Minkowski [F4] gives $\|s_m\|_2\le\sum_{k=1}^m2^{-k}\le1$. The functions $s_m^2$ increase, so monotone convergence [F4] yields $\int(\lim_m s_m)^2\,d\rho\le1$. Therefore $\sum_kd_k(y)<\infty$ outside a measurable null set; otherwise its square integral would be infinite on a set of positive measure.

Let $E=\{y:\sum_kd_k(y)<\infty\}$, a Borel set of full measure by step 1.2. On $E$, $(U_{n_k}(y))$ is Cauchy in $V$ and hence has a limit by [F2]. Define $U(y)$ to be this limit on $E$ and zero on $E^c$. The Borel maps equal to $U_{n_k}$ on $E$ and zero on $E^c$ converge pointwise everywhere to $U$; their pointwise limit is Borel measurable (equivalently, distances to a countable dense subset of $V$ are Borel limits). By [F5], $U$ is strongly measurable. If $g_m=\sum_{k\ge m}d_k$, then $g_m\downarrow0$ almost everywhere, $g_m\le\lim_k s_k$, and the latter is in $L^2$ by step 1.2. Dominated convergence [F6] gives $\|g_m\|_2\to0$, while $\|U-U_{n_m}\|_V\le g_m$ almost everywhere on $E$. Thus $U_{n_m}\to U$ in $L^2_\rho(V)$.

Since $(U_n)$ is Cauchy and its subsequence converges to $U$, the full sequence converges to $U$: for $\varepsilon>0$, choose $N$ so $\|U_n-U_m\|<\varepsilon/2$ for $m,n\ge N$, then choose $n_k\ge N$ with $\|U_{n_k}-U\|<\varepsilon/2$; the triangle inequality gives $\|U_n-U\|<\varepsilon$ for $n\ge N$. Let $U\in L^2_\rho(V)$ and choose a strongly measurable representative with simple approximants and measurable null exceptional set as in the definition. Dominated convergence [F6] gives convergence in $L^2_\rho(V)$, proving density.

Let $D\subset\mathbb R^m$ be a bounded polyhedral open set and
$V=H_0^1(D;\mathbb R)$ with norm $\|v\|_V=\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(D)}$.
[[lem-parabolic-zero-boundary-sobolev-space-is-separable]] supplies the
separable Hilbert structure under Countable Choice; the gradient norm is
equivalent to its Sobolev norm there.

Let $Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_d)$ have the product law $\rho$ of
[[def-finite-product-chaos-input]], and assume its support $\Gamma$ is bounded,
so $|y_j|\le R_j<\infty$ for every $y\in\Gamma$.
For real coefficient functions $a_0,\ldots,a_d\in L^\infty(D)$ define
$$a(x,y)=a_0(x)+\sum_{j=1}^d y_j a_j(x).$$
Assume constants $0<a_*\le a^*<\infty$ satisfy, for every $y\in\Gamma$,
$a_*\le a(x,y)\le a^*$ for almost every $x\in D$. This explicit
all-parameter condition ensures the pointwise variational problem is
well-posed for every stated parameter, not merely almost every one. Let
$F(y)=f_0+\sum_{j=1}^d y_j f_j$ with $f_j\in V^*$.

The pointwise weak form is
$$a_y(u,v)=\int_Da(x,y)\nabla u(x)\cdot\nabla v(x)\,dx=F(y)(v),\qquad v\in V.$$
The Bochner weak form uses the bilinear form
$$\mathcal A(U,W)=\int_\Gamma a_y(U(y),W(y))\,d\rho(y)$$
and the functional $\mathcal F(W)=\int_\Gamma F(y)(W(y))\,d\rho(y)$ on
$L^2_\rho(V)$ from [[def-finite-input-bochner-l2-space]].

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A function $f:\Omega\to X$ is **strongly measurable** (or
**Bochner measurable**) if there are measurable $X$-valued simple functions
$s_n$ and a measurable null set $N$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\|s_n(\omega)-f(\omega)\|=0$$

for every $\omega\in\Omega\setminus N$.

This is a norm-convergence condition. It is not, by definition, merely Borel
measurability of $f$ or measurability of every scalar function $x^*\circ f$.
Changing $f$ on a null set preserves strong measurability: enlarge $N$ by that
null set and retain the same approximants.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Let $(\Gamma,\mathcal B(\Gamma),\rho)$ be the finite product-law probability
space of [[def-finite-product-chaos-input]], and let $V$ be a separable real
Hilbert space. Define $L^2_\rho(V)$ to be the space of strongly measurable
maps $U:\Gamma\to V$ for which
$\int_\Gamma\|U(y)\|_V^2\,d\rho(y)<\infty$, modulo equality
$\rho$-almost everywhere. Its inner product is
$$ (U,W)_{L^2_\rho(V)}=\int_\Gamma (U(y),W(y))_V\,d\rho(y). $$

derivations.claim: Choose finite-valued measurable simple maps $U_n,W_n$ converging respectively to $U,W$ almost everywhere, using [F2]. On every intersection of their finite partition sets, $y\mapsto a_y(U_n(y),W_n(y))$ is an affine continuous scalar function of $y$ by the displayed coefficient formula in [F1]. It is therefore measurable. On the common full-measure set where both approximations converge, continuity of the bounded bilinear form gives convergence to $a_y(U(y),W(y))$. Defining the scalar function arbitrarily on the measurable exceptional null set gives a measurable representative.

For a finite-valued simple $W_n$ converging almost everywhere to $W$, the scalar function $F(y)(W_n(y))$ is measurable on each partition piece because $F(y)$ is affine continuous into the finite-dimensional span of $f_0,\ldots,f_d$. Its pointwise limit on the full-measure convergence set is $F(y)(W(y))$, so the latter has a measurable representative. Since $|y_j|\le R_j$, $\|F(y)\|_{V^*}\le\|f_0\|_{V^*}+\sum_jR_j\|f_j\|_{V^*}$; hence $F\in L^2_\rho(V^*)$.

The pointwise bound [F1] gives $|a_y(U(y),W(y))|\le a^*\|U(y)\|_V\|W(y)\|_V$. Both norm functions are square-integrable, so [F3] makes this majorant integrable. The form integral is finite and depends only on the almost-everywhere classes by [F4].
Pointwise duality gives $|F(y)(W(y))|\le\|F(y)\|_{V^*}\|W(y)\|_V$. Apply [F3] to obtain the stated integrability and functional bound.

Integrating the pointwise coercivity bound [F1] gives $\mathcal A(U,U)\ge a_*\int\|U(y)\|_V^2\,d\rho=a_*\|U\|_{\mathcal H}^2$. Integrating the pointwise continuity bound and applying [F3] as in step 2.1 gives $|\mathcal A(U,W)|\le a^*\|U\|_{\mathcal H}\|W\|_{\mathcal H}$. These estimates prove the remaining assertions.

[[def-finite-product-chaos-input]]. The monomial classes
$1,y,\ldots,y^{p_j}$ are linearly independent in $L^2(\rho_j)$. Applying the
finite Gram–Schmidt recursion to this ordered list gives real orthonormal
polynomials $\phi_{j,0},\ldots,\phi_{j,p_j}$, where $\phi_{j,k}$ has degree
$k$, positive leading coefficient, and $\phi_{j,0}=1$.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

$$G=\frac1M\sum_{i=1}^M\frac{N}{K_\Lambda(X_i)}\psi(X_i)\psi(X_i)^T,\qquad b=\frac1M\sum_{i=1}^M\frac{N}{K_\Lambda(X_i)}u(X_i)\psi(X_i).$$

$$\frac1M\sum_{i=1}^M\frac{N}{K_\Lambda(X_i)}|u(X_i)-p(X_i)|^2,$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded
polyhedral open set with $d\ge1$. Put
$$H=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R),\qquad V=W^{1,2}_0(\Omega;\mathbb R),\qquad \|v\|_V=\|v\|_{W^{1,2}(\Omega)}.$$
Then $V$ is a separable real Hilbert space, and the inclusion
$V\hookrightarrow H$ is continuous, injective and dense. Consequently
$(V,H,V^*)$ is a real evolution triple in the sense of
[[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]]. The gradient norm
$\|\nabla v\|_{L^2}$ is equivalent to this norm on $V$ by Poincare's
inequality.

Let $D\subset\mathbb R^m$ be a bounded polyhedral open set and
$V=H_0^1(D;\mathbb R)$ with norm $\|v\|_V=\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(D)}$.
[[lem-parabolic-zero-boundary-sobolev-space-is-separable]] supplies the
separable Hilbert structure under Countable Choice; the gradient norm is
equivalent to its Sobolev norm there.

Let $Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_d)$ have the product law $\rho$ of
[[def-finite-product-chaos-input]], and assume its support $\Gamma$ is bounded,
so $|y_j|\le R_j<\infty$ for every $y\in\Gamma$.
For real coefficient functions $a_0,\ldots,a_d\in L^\infty(D)$ define
$$a(x,y)=a_0(x)+\sum_{j=1}^d y_j a_j(x).$$
Assume constants $0<a_*\le a^*<\infty$ satisfy, for every $y\in\Gamma$,
$a_*\le a(x,y)\le a^*$ for almost every $x\in D$. This explicit
all-parameter condition ensures the pointwise variational problem is
well-posed for every stated parameter, not merely almost every one. Let
$F(y)=f_0+\sum_{j=1}^d y_j f_j$ with $f_j\in V^*$.

The pointwise weak form is
$$a_y(u,v)=\int_Da(x,y)\nabla u(x)\cdot\nabla v(x)\,dx=F(y)(v),\qquad v\in V.$$
The Bochner weak form uses the bilinear form
$$\mathcal A(U,W)=\int_\Gamma a_y(U(y),W(y))\,d\rho(y)$$
and the functional $\mathcal F(W)=\int_\Gamma F(y)(W(y))\,d\rho(y)$ on
$L^2_\rho(V)$ from [[def-finite-input-bochner-l2-space]].

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. The real bilinear case is the same statement with $a$ symmetric or not, $F$ a bounded linear functional, and the conjugation read as the identity.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Banach space, and let $f:\Omega\to B$ be Borel-measurable. Then $f$ is strongly
measurable: outside a $P$-null set it is the pointwise limit of finite-valued

Lax–Milgram gives a unique $u(y)\in V$ and $\|u(y)\|_V\le F_{\max}/a_*$, where $F_{\max}:=\sup_{y\in\Gamma}\|F(y)\|_{V^*}<\infty$ because $\Gamma$ is bounded.

For $y,z\in\Gamma$, put $d=u(y)-u(z)$ and subtract the weak equations: $a_y(d,v)=(F(y)-F(z))(v)+(a_z-a_y)(u(z),v).$ The affine formulas give $\|F(y)-F(z)\|_{V^*}\le C_F\|y-z\|_1$ and $|a_z(v,w)-a_y(v,w)|\le C_a\|y-z\|_1\|v\|_V\|w\|_V$, where $C_F=\sum_j\|f_j\|_{V^*}$ and $C_a=\sum_j\|a_j\|_{L^\infty(D)}$. $$ (U,W)_{L^2_\rho(V)}=\int_\Gamma (U(y),W(y))_V\,d\rho(y). $$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A function $f:\Omega\to X$ is **strongly measurable** (or
**Bochner measurable**) if there are measurable $X$-valued simple functions
$s_n$ and a measurable null set $N$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\|s_n(\omega)-f(\omega)\|=0$$

for every $\omega\in\Omega\setminus N$.

This is a norm-convergence condition. It is not, by definition, merely Borel
measurability of $f$ or measurability of every scalar function $x^*\circ f$.
Changing $f$ on a null set preserves strong measurability: enlarge $N$ by that
null set and retain the same approximants.

Because there are finitely many values, it is enough to approximate each term $\mathbf1_{E_k}v_k$ so that the sum of its errors is less than $\varepsilon/2$.

For each $k$, use [F3] and [F4] to choose $s_k\in\mathcal S$ and $w_k\in V_0$ with $\|\mathbf1_{E_k}-s_k\|_{L^2(\rho)}\|v_k\|_V+ \|s_k\|_{L^2(\rho)}\|v_k-w_k\|_V<\varepsilon/(2m)$. Such choices are possible by first making the scalar error arbitrarily small, which bounds $\|s_k\|_2\le\|\mathbf1_{E_k}\|_2+\|\mathbf1_{E_k}-s_k\|_2$, and then making the vector error small. The product norm estimate $\|\mathbf1_{E_k}v_k-s_kw_k\|_{L^2_\rho(V)} \le\|\mathbf1_{E_k}-s_k\|_2\|v_k\|_V+\|s_k\|_2\|v_k-w_k\|_V$ follows pointwise from the triangle inequality and then from scalar square-integral estimation. Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A function $f:\Omega\to X$ is **strongly measurable** (or
**Bochner measurable**) if there are measurable $X$-valued simple functions
$s_n$ and a measurable null set $N$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\|s_n(\omega)-f(\omega)\|=0$$

for every $\omega\in\Omega\setminus N$.

This is a norm-convergence condition. It is not, by definition, merely Borel
measurability of $f$ or measurability of every scalar function $x^*\circ f$.
Changing $f$ on a null set preserves strong measurability: enlarge $N$ by that
null set and retain the same approximants.

$$|a(v,w)|\le M\|v\|_V\|w\|_V,\qquad \operatorname{Re}a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|_V^2.$$

$$a(u_h,v_h)=F(v_h)\quad(v_h\in V_h).$$

$$\|u-u_h\|_V\le\frac M\alpha\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_V.$$

Use the dyadic composite-Simpson hierarchy of
[[def-smolyak-univariate-level-hierarchy]]. Let $d\ge1$. For
$S=\{j_1<\cdots<j_k\}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}$, define
$$D_Sf:=\partial_{x_{j_k}}^4\cdots\partial_{x_{j_1}}^4f,$$
so these derivatives are applied in increasing coordinate order; set
$D_\varnothing f=f$. Assume every $D_Sf$ is continuous on the closed cube,
with the one-sided endpoint convention of
[[def-higher-derivatives-and-smoothness]], and choose finite bounds $M_S\ge0$
such that $|D_Sf(x)|\le M_S$ on $[0,1]^d$. For
$\ell\in\mathbb N_0^d$, put $S(\ell):=\{j:\ell_j\ge1\}$ and
$$\delta_\ell(f):=(\Delta_{\ell_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes\Delta_{\ell_d}^{(d)})(f).$$

$$|\delta_\ell(f)|\le M_{S(\ell)}\left(\frac{17}{2880}\right)^{|S(\ell)|}16^{-\sum_{j\in S(\ell)}\ell_j}.$$

$$\sum_{\ell\in F}|\delta_\ell(f)|\le\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}}M_S\left(\frac{17}{43200}\right)^{|S|}<\infty.$$

Fix a dimension $d\ge1$. A finite set $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb N_0^d$ is
**downward closed** if, whenever $\ell\in\Lambda$ and $\ell_j>0$, the index
$\ell-e_j$ also belongs to $\Lambda$; here $e_j$ is the $j$th coordinate unit
vector. In this pair an admissible Smolyak set is a nonempty finite downward-
closed $\Lambda$ that contains $0$.

For a level hierarchy from [[def-smolyak-univariate-level-hierarchy]], define
the **Smolyak cubature functional**
$$Q_\Lambda(f):=\sum_{\ell\in\Lambda}(\Delta_{\ell_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes\Delta_{\ell_d}^{(d)})(f).$$
Each summand is a finite signed weighted sum. Expanding all differences and
adding coefficients at equal points gives one finite signed weight for each
distinct node in
$$\mathcal N_\Lambda:=\bigcup_{\ell\in\Lambda}X_{\ell_1}\times\cdots\times X_{\ell_d}.$$
The **node-union work count** for this direct evaluation convention is
$W(\Lambda):=|\mathcal N_\Lambda|$, so shared nodes are counted once. A
combined weight may be negative or zero; no positivity claim follows from the
definition.

[[def-finite-chaos-orthogonal-projection]] and
[[def-chaos-quadrature-coefficient-estimator]], with $\widetilde u$ as the

$$G=\frac1M\sum_{i=1}^M\frac{N}{K_\Lambda(X_i)}\psi(X_i)\psi(X_i)^T,\qquad b=\frac1M\sum_{i=1}^M\frac{N}{K_\Lambda(X_i)}u(X_i)\psi(X_i).$$

Fix an integer $d\ge1$, independent real random variables
$Y_1,\ldots,Y_d$ with marginal Borel probability laws $\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_d$,
and a degree cutoff vector $p=(p_1,\ldots,p_d)\in\mathbb N_0^d$. Their joint
law is $\rho=\rho_1\otimes\cdots\otimes\rho_d$, as in
[[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]]. Write
$\Gamma=\prod_{j=1}^d\operatorname{supp}(\rho_j)$, with the product Borel
sigma-algebra. The cutoff vector $p$ is **admissible** when, for every
$j=1,\ldots,d$,
$$\int |y|^{2p_j}\,d\rho_j(y)<\infty$$
and the monomial Gram matrix
$$G_j=(\int y^{r+s}\,d\rho_j(y))_{0\le r,s\le p_j}$$
is positive definite, meaning $c^T G_jc>0$ for each nonzero
$c\in\mathbb R^{p_j+1}$. Throughout the pair, assume the selected cutoff
vector is admissible. The admissible degree box is
$\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^d:0\le\alpha_j\le p_j\text{ for every }j\}$.
Admissibility gives a finite inner product on each stated polynomial space.
It is only a finite-degree condition; it does not assert that polynomials are
dense in any $L^2(\rho_j)$.

Let $\phi_{j,k}$ be the Gram–Schmidt polynomials from
[[lem-positive-moment-gram-produces-univariate-chaos-polynomials]], and let
$\Lambda$ be a finite subset of the admissible degree box in
[[def-finite-product-chaos-input]]. For $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d)\in\Lambda$,

$$\psi_\alpha(y_1,\ldots,y_d)=\prod_{j=1}^d\phi_{j,\alpha_j}(y_j).$$
The **finite polynomial-chaos space** is
$\mathcal P_\Lambda=\operatorname{span}\{\psi_\alpha:\alpha\in\Lambda\}$
inside $L^2(\rho)$. Whenever $0\in\Lambda$ (in particular, for the stated
total-degree and hyperbolic-cross sets), the family contains the constant mode
$\psi_0=1$. No density of $\mathcal P_\Lambda$ in $L^2(\rho)$ is part of this
definition.

random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

For $d\ge1$, let $(a_j,b_j,m_j,2m_j-1,\mu_j)$ be Gaussian moment data for
each coordinate $j=1,\ldots,d$, and write
$M^{(j)}_k:=\int x^k\,d\mu_j(x)$. A **coordinatewise tensor polynomial** is a
finite family $(c_\alpha)$, with $c_\alpha\in\mathbb R$ for every index, indexed by multi-indices
$\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d)$ with
$0\le\alpha_j\le2m_j-1$, evaluated by
$$ P(x_1,\ldots,x_d)=\sum_{\alpha}c_\alpha\prod_{j=1}^{d}x_j^{\alpha_j}. $$
Define its **coordinatewise product-moment value** by
$$ I_\otimes(P):=\sum_{\alpha}c_\alpha\prod_{j=1}^{d}M^{(j)}_{\alpha_j}. $$
In both sums, list the finite multi-index box in increasing lexicographic
order (coordinate $1$ first, then coordinate $2$, and so on), and take the
ordinary finite-list sum in that order. The products use increasing coordinate
order $j=1,\ldots,d$. The real coefficient family is part of the formal
polynomial data, so these formulas specify finite real sums. This definition specifies the product-moment functional
used for coordinatewise exactness without requiring a measure-product
construction.

For the Gaussian coordinate data of [[def-coordinatewise-product-moment-functional]], let $\mu=\mu_1\otimes\cdots\otimes\mu_d$ on the finite product of the relative Borel interval spaces, with binary products iterated from left to right. Every real coordinatewise tensor polynomial $P$ in that definition is integrable and
$$\int P\,d\mu=I_\otimes(P).$$
This supplies a measure interpretation of the algebraic functional without redefining it. The conclusion also applies when each marginal measure is a probability law.

For $d\ge1$, take one-dimensional Gaussian rules $Q_j$ with orders $m_j$ and
moment data $(a_j,b_j,m_j,2m_j-1,\mu_j)$, and form their tensor rule
$Q_\otimes$ as in [[def-tensor-product-gauss-rule]]. For every coordinatewise
tensor polynomial $P$ of [[def-coordinatewise-product-moment-functional]],
$$ Q_\otimes(P)=I_\otimes(P). $$
The tensor rule has exactly $\prod_{j=1}^{d}m_j$ distinct nodes. In particular,
using the same $m\ge2$ nodes in each coordinate requires $m^d$ node
evaluations, exponential growth in $d$.

Let $\rho=\otimes_{j=1}^d\rho_j$ and form $\psi_\alpha$ from
[[def-chaos-orthonormal-tensor-basis]] for indices in the admissible degree
box. Then each $\psi_\alpha$ belongs to
$L^2(\rho)$ and
$$\int_\Gamma\psi_\alpha(y)\psi_\beta(y)\,d\rho(y)=\begin{cases}1,&\alpha=\beta,\\0,&\alpha\ne\beta.\end{cases}$$
In particular, the family indexed by any finite subset $\Lambda$ of the box is
orthonormal; when $0\in\Lambda$, it includes the constant mode $\psi_0=1$.

Let $\Lambda$ be a finite index set and let $Q$ be any declared finite
cubature functional
$Q(g)=\sum_{q=1}^Jw_qg(y^{(q)})$ whose nodes lie in the domain of evaluation
of $g$. For an evaluable real function $u$, define the quadrature coefficient
and the resulting polynomial by
$$\widehat c_\alpha:=Q(u\psi_\alpha),\qquad \widehat P_\Lambda u:=\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda}\widehat c_\alpha\psi_\alpha.$$
The exact coefficients $c_\alpha$ and projection $P_\Lambda u$ are those of
[[def-finite-chaos-orthogonal-projection]]. This definition gives no
accuracy claim for a general cubature rule.

derivations.claim: Expand $u=\sum_{\beta\in\Lambda}c_\beta\psi_\beta$. By [F1] and [F2], each $\psi_\beta$ has coordinate degree $\beta_j\le p_j$, so each product $\psi_\beta\psi_\alpha$ has degree at most $2p_j\le2m_j-2\le2m_j-1$ in coordinate $j$.

By [F3] and [F4], the product-law integral of this finite polynomial equals its coordinatewise product-moment functional. Its degrees satisfy the limits checked in step 1.1, so [F5] gives $Q_\otimes(\psi_\beta\psi_\alpha)=\int\psi_\beta\psi_\alpha\,d\rho=\delta_{\alpha\beta}$ by [F6]. Finite linearity then gives $Q_\otimes(u\psi_\alpha)=c_\alpha=\langle u,\psi_\alpha\rangle$.

The equality in step 2.1 holds for every $\alpha\in\Lambda$, so all coefficient differences vanish and the finite sums defining $\widehat P_\Lambda u$ and $P_\Lambda u$ coincide. The quadrature contribution in the error split is therefore zero.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$, independent real random variables
$Y_1,\ldots,Y_d$ with marginal Borel probability laws $\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_d$,
and a degree cutoff vector $p=(p_1,\ldots,p_d)\in\mathbb N_0^d$. Their joint
law is $\rho=\rho_1\otimes\cdots\otimes\rho_d$, as in
[[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]]. Write
$\Gamma=\prod_{j=1}^d\operatorname{supp}(\rho_j)$, with the product Borel
sigma-algebra. The cutoff vector $p$ is **admissible** when, for every
$j=1,\ldots,d$,
$$\int |y|^{2p_j}\,d\rho_j(y)<\infty$$
and the monomial Gram matrix
$$G_j=(\int y^{r+s}\,d\rho_j(y))_{0\le r,s\le p_j}$$
is positive definite, meaning $c^T G_jc>0$ for each nonzero
$c\in\mathbb R^{p_j+1}$. Throughout the pair, assume the selected cutoff
vector is admissible. The admissible degree box is
$\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^d:0\le\alpha_j\le p_j\text{ for every }j\}$.
Admissibility gives a finite inner product on each stated polynomial space.
It is only a finite-degree condition; it does not assert that polynomials are
dense in any $L^2(\rho_j)$.

Let $D\subset\mathbb R^m$ be a bounded polyhedral open set and
$V=H_0^1(D;\mathbb R)$ with norm $\|v\|_V=\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(D)}$.
[[lem-parabolic-zero-boundary-sobolev-space-is-separable]] supplies the
separable Hilbert structure under Countable Choice; the gradient norm is
equivalent to its Sobolev norm there.

Let $Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_d)$ have the product law $\rho$ of
[[def-finite-product-chaos-input]], and assume its support $\Gamma$ is bounded,
so $|y_j|\le R_j<\infty$ for every $y\in\Gamma$.
For real coefficient functions $a_0,\ldots,a_d\in L^\infty(D)$ define
$$a(x,y)=a_0(x)+\sum_{j=1}^d y_j a_j(x).$$
Assume constants $0<a_*\le a^*<\infty$ satisfy, for every $y\in\Gamma$,
$a_*\le a(x,y)\le a^*$ for almost every $x\in D$. This explicit
all-parameter condition ensures the pointwise variational problem is
well-posed for every stated parameter, not merely almost every one. Let
$F(y)=f_0+\sum_{j=1}^d y_j f_j$ with $f_j\in V^*$.

The pointwise weak form is
$$a_y(u,v)=\int_Da(x,y)\nabla u(x)\cdot\nabla v(x)\,dx=F(y)(v),\qquad v\in V.$$
The Bochner weak form uses the bilinear form
$$\mathcal A(U,W)=\int_\Gamma a_y(U(y),W(y))\,d\rho(y)$$
and the functional $\mathcal F(W)=\int_\Gamma F(y)(W(y))\,d\rho(y)$ on
$L^2_\rho(V)$ from [[def-finite-input-bochner-l2-space]].

Under the hypotheses of [[def-uniformly-elliptic-affine-random-diffusion]],
for each $y\in\Gamma$ there is a unique $u(y)\in V$ satisfying the pointwise
weak problem. The map $y\mapsto u(y)$ is Lipschitz on the bounded parameter
set, strongly measurable, and belongs to $L^2_\rho(V)$. It is also the unique
solution of the Bochner weak equation
$$\mathcal A(u,W)=\mathcal F(W)\qquad(W\in L^2_\rho(V)).$$

derivations.claim: At cutoff $p_1=0$, the only moment-Gram matrix is $[1]$, so the uniform probability law is admissible by [F1]. Its support is $\Gamma=[-1,1]$, and for every $y\in\Gamma$, $1\le2+y\le3$. Thus the diffusion definition applies with $a_*=1$ and $a^*=3$, and $F=0$ is a bounded affine forcing.

The pointwise weak equation is $\int_0^1(2+y)u'(x)v'(x)\,dx=0$ for every $v\in H_0^1(0,1)$. Taking $v=u$ and using $2+y\ge1$ gives $\|u\|_{H_0^1}^2\le0$, so $u=0$ for every $y$. This solution is a strongly measurable square-integrable zero function and satisfies the Bochner equation; uniqueness also follows from [F3].

Let $\rho_j$ be one factor law with admissible degree $p_j$ as in
[[def-finite-product-chaos-input]]. The monomial classes
$1,y,\ldots,y^{p_j}$ are linearly independent in $L^2(\rho_j)$. Applying the
finite Gram–Schmidt recursion to this ordered list gives real orthonormal
polynomials $\phi_{j,0},\ldots,\phi_{j,p_j}$, where $\phi_{j,k}$ has degree
$k$, positive leading coefficient, and $\phi_{j,0}=1$.

Let $\Lambda$ be finite, contain $0$, and let the real basis
$(\psi_\alpha)_{\alpha\in\Lambda}$ be as in
[[def-chaos-orthonormal-tensor-basis]]. For real $u\in L^2(\rho)$ set
$c_\alpha=\langle u,\psi_\alpha\rangle$ and
$P_\Lambda u=\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda}c_\alpha\psi_\alpha$ as in
[[def-finite-chaos-orthogonal-projection]]. Then
$$\|u\|_{L^2(\rho)}^2=\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda}c_\alpha^2+ \|u-P_\Lambda u\|_{L^2(\rho)}^2.$$
The residual is orthogonal to $\mathcal P_\Lambda$,
$\mathbb E[u]=c_0$, and
$$\operatorname{Var}(u)=\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda\setminus\{0\}}c_\alpha^2+ \|u-P_\Lambda u\|_{L^2(\rho)}^2.$$
Here $\operatorname{Var}(u)=\mathbb E[(u-\mathbb E u)^2]$; no completeness of
the polynomial family is assumed.

derivations.claim: The first two moments are $\mathbb E[Y]=0$ and $\mathbb E[Y^2]=1$, so the degree-one Gram matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, positive definite. Thus [F1] applies. Gram--Schmidt gives $\psi_0=1$ and $\psi_1=Y$, since $Y$ already has mean zero and unit norm and its leading coefficient is positive.

Substitution gives $k(Y)=\kappa\psi_0+\kappa\eta\psi_1$ at both support points, so the degree-one projection residual is identically zero. Its coefficients are $c_0=\mathbb E[k(Y)]=\kappa$ and $c_1=\mathbb E[k(Y)Y]=\kappa\eta$. By [F3], the mean is $c_0$ and variance is $c_1^2=\kappa^2\eta^2$.

The condition $|\eta|<1$ implies $1+\eta Y\ge1-|\eta|>0$ at both states, so the reaction rate is positive on its whole support. Every function on this support also has the exact form $g(Y)=\frac{g(1)+g(-1)}2+\frac{g(1)-g(-1)}2Y$; hence this two-dimensional finite basis spans $L^2(\rho)$ for this particular law.

$p=(p_1,\ldots,p_d)$ from [[def-finite-product-chaos-input]], the cutoff
total-degree set of order $s\ge0$ and cutoff hyperbolic-cross set of
threshold $N\ge1$ are
$$\Lambda^{\mathrm{TD}}_{s,p}=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^d:0\le\alpha_j\le p_j,\ \sum_{j=1}^d\alpha_j\le s\},\qquad \Lambda^{\mathrm{HC}}_{N,p}=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^d:0\le\alpha_j\le p_j,\ \prod_{j=1}^d(\alpha_j+1)\le N\},$$
The cutoff vector prevents either set from requesting
polynomials above the moment degree declared in
[[def-finite-product-chaos-input]]. Both are finite and contain zero.
An arbitrary finite index set used below is denoted by $\Lambda$; whenever a
downward-closed set is required, this means $\alpha\in\Lambda$ and
$0\le\beta_j\le\alpha_j$ for every $j$ imply $\beta\in\Lambda$.

For every admissible cutoff vector $p\in\mathbb N_0^d$, order $s\ge0$, and
threshold $N\ge1$, the sets $\Lambda^{\mathrm{TD}}_{s,p}$ and
$\Lambda^{\mathrm{HC}}_{N,p}$ of
[[def-chaos-total-degree-and-hyperbolic-cross-index-sets]] are finite and
contain $0$.

For $d\ge1$, take one-dimensional Gaussian rules $Q_j$ with orders $m_j$ and
moment data $(a_j,b_j,m_j,2m_j-1,\mu_j)$, and form their tensor rule
$Q_\otimes$ as in [[def-tensor-product-gauss-rule]]. For every coordinatewise
tensor polynomial $P$ of [[def-coordinatewise-product-moment-functional]],
$$ Q_\otimes(P)=I_\otimes(P). $$
The tensor rule has exactly $\prod_{j=1}^{d}m_j$ distinct nodes. In particular,
using the same $m\ge2$ nodes in each coordinate requires $m^d$ node
evaluations, exponential growth in $d$.

derivations.claim: For one uniform marginal, the moment Gram matrix through degree two is $\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1/3\\0&1/3&0\\1/3&0&1/5\end{pmatrix}$. Its quadratic form at $(c_0,c_1,c_2)$ is $(c_0+c_2/3)^2+c_1^2/3+4c_2^2/45$, which is positive for every nonzero vector; all required moments are finite on $[-1,1]$. Thus the cutoff is admissible. In three coordinates, the total-degree set has one zero multi-index, three degree-one indices, three indices $2e_j$, and three indices $e_i+e_j$ with $i<j$. These are disjoint and exhaust the nonnegative triples with sum at most two, so its cardinality is $1+3+3+3=10$.

The full degree-two tensor box has $3$ choices in each of three coordinates, hence $3^3=27$ multi-indices. The three-node Gaussian rules are defined for the positive uniform measures on $[-1,1]$; their tensor rule with $m_1=m_2=m_3=3$ has $3^3=27$ distinct nodes by [F3]. Thus in this example the total-degree basis uses ten modes compared with twenty-seven tensor modes and node evaluations.
